bangus.description: This fish has a slender, slightly compressed body that tapers to a large, deeply forked tail. Its mouth is small and lacks teeth, and it possesses a single dorsal fin positioned roughly halfway along its back, supported by two spines and between thirteen and seventeen soft rays. The anal fin has two spines and eight to ten soft rays, while the pectoral fins are curved like a sickle. The belly is smooth, without any bony scutes, and it has four branchiostegal rays beneath the gills. In total, the species has forty‑six vertebrae. Its coloration is olive‑green on the top, silvery along the sides, and the unpaired fins are outlined with dark margins. The overall shape is elongated with an oval cross‑section.

budlis.description: This fish has a streamlined, elongated body that is rounded in cross‑section. Its dorsal fin is made up of 14 to 16 spines followed by 14 to 15 soft rays, and the two dorsal fins are separated by a very small gap no larger than the eye; the second dorsal fin is followed by seven to nine small finlets. The anal fin lacks spines and contains 14 to 15 soft rays, with eight or so finlets behind it. It has 26–27 short rays in each pectoral fin and two small flaps between the pelvic fins. The mouth holds small, cone‑shaped teeth arranged in a single row, and the first gill arch bears many gill rakers—about fifty‑three to sixty‑three. The fish’s skeleton includes 41 vertebrae. Its body is mostly scaleless except for a bony band (corselet) and the lateral line, and each side of the caudal‑fin base has a prominent keel flanked by two smaller keels. In life, the back is a dark purplish‑blue while the lower sides and belly are silvery, marked with four to six striking longitudinal dark bands that may appear as a series of dark blotches.

tamban.description: The fish has no dorsal spines and between thirteen and twenty‑one soft rays on its dorsal fin, while the anal fin lacks spines and bears roughly twelve to twenty‑three soft rays. A subtle golden spot sits just behind the gill opening, followed by a faint golden line that runs along the middle of its side, and a distinct black spot marks the rear edge of the gill cover where pigment is absent. Its body is elongated and almost cylindrical in shape, giving it a streamlined, fusiform appearance that is laterally compressed. This species can be distinguished from other clupeids in the eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific by the number of rays in its pelvic fin, and it differs from *Scomberomorus longiceps* by having a shorter head and fewer lower‑gill rakers.

tilapia.description: The fish is a relatively large, deep‑bodied tilapia with a slender, laterally‑compressed shape. It has 15 to 18 spiny rays on its dorsal fin and 11 to 13 soft rays on the same fin, while the anal fin carries three spines and nine to eleven soft rays. Its total vertebrae count ranges from 30 to 32. The head is proportionally small, making up only a modest part of the body length, and even mature males have jaws that are not dramatically enlarged—the lower jaw is about 30‑37 % of the head length. Breeding males lack a tassel‑like genital papilla. The body is quite tall, with a depth that measures roughly one‑third to one‑half of the standard length. A key identifying feature is the presence of regular vertical stripes that run the full height of the tail fin at every life stage; in younger fish these stripes are wider, form an arc, and begin at the base of the tail. Males typically display a bluish‑pink coloration, sometimes with darker throats and darker anal and pelvic fins, whereas females are generally brownish on top with silvery‑white undersides and about ten thin vertical bars.

sagision.description: The fish has a total of ten dorsal spines and nine soft rays on its dorsal fin, together with three spines and seven soft rays on its anal fin. It lacks a suborbital spine, and its preopercle is covered by three rows of scales running across it. Its pectoral fins are long, extending to a point between the anus and the start of the anal fin, while the pelvic fins are even longer, reaching the level of, or extending beyond, the origin of the anal fin. The upper lobe of the caudal fin is slightly rounded and bears a rosy hue. A distinct line runs upward from the rear edge of the suborbital area and meets the dorsal profile about two to four scales before the dorsal fin begins. An axillary scale is present. In coloration, the upper part of the body is pinkish, transitioning to a silvery‑white shade on the underside. Two silvery‑mauve lines run in front of and below the eye. The fish’s body is fusiform and of normal shape, with an oval cross‑section.

burao.description: The fish has a streamlined, fusiform body with an oval cross‑section. Its head is noticeably longer than the depth of its body, and the maxilla is covered by the lachrymal bone. It possesses a swim bladder and a small, single interpelvic process, while the anal spine is only rudimentary. The dorsal fin is supported by eight to eleven spines and twelve soft rays, and the anal fin has twelve soft rays with no spines. In total, the species has thirty‑one vertebrae. Its gill rakers are bristly, with thirty to fifty‑five on each side, but they do not extend far into the mouth. A distinctive black blotch sits just behind the base of the pectoral fin, and the belly displays a yellowish‑silver hue. Between two and six large spots often appear at the base of the first dorsal fin, and some individuals show two faint stripes along the lateral line.

talho.description: The fish has no dorsal spines and about eleven or twelve soft rays on its dorsal fin, with a similar number of soft rays on its anal fin and no anal spines. Its body is cigar‑shaped, either rounded or slightly flattened, and its head is pointed and low‑set with a rounded snout. The dorsal fin starts nearer the small, fleshy adipose fin than it does the tip of the snout, while the anal fin begins closer to the base of the tail than to the gill cover. The fish’s coloration is a brown‑gray shade on the upper side that fades to a creamy tone underneath, and it bears eight to ten faint darker spots running along the middle of its sides. Overall, the fish has an elongated, circular‑cross‑section body shape.

sapsap.description: This fish has a deep, laterally‑compressed body with a strongly humped back, giving it a very tall profile—its depth is roughly half its length. Its mouth points downward when it opens. The dorsal fin is supported by eight spines and fifteen to sixteen soft rays, while the anal fin has three spines and fourteen to fifteen soft rays. The first gill arch bears eighteen to twenty‑two short, fleshy gill rakers that are less than half the length of the gill filaments. The head and breast are smooth and scaleless, and the lateral line is lined with sixty‑one to sixty‑six tubular scales. Adults are greyish on the back, silvery on the belly, and display many faint, closely spaced parallel bars across the back, often with a dark brown saddle marking on the caudal peduncle. The area under the pectoral fins (axil) ranges from grey to black, the soft dorsal fin has a black margin, and both lobes of the tail fin have broad, dusky edges. The pectoral, pelvic, and anal fins are colorless to yellowish. Juveniles, about five to seven centimeters long, are marked by thin, closely spaced grey vertical lines that run from the back down to about mid‑height; the membrane between the anal‑fin spines is conspicuously yellow, the rear edges of the tail‑fin lobes are pale yellow with dusky shading, the other fins are transparent, and the snout bears small black dots.

moonfish.description: This fish has a very deep, almost triangular body that is extremely laterally compressed, giving it a sharp‑edged breast. Its deepest point lies below the lateral line and is at least four times deeper than the shallowest point above the line. The anal fin is unusually long, starting where the pelvic fins attach, and runs low along the body. Juveniles have ten dorsal spines, but the number drops to three or four as they grow, while the dorsal fin carries about 40 to 45 soft rays and the anal fin has 30 to 33 soft rays with no spines. Its coloration is striking: the upper sides are a deep metallic blue, the rest of the body is silvery, and a series of round‑to‑oval dark slate‑blue spots run above and below the lateral line, sometimes with a few extra spots nearby. The pelvic fins show a faint hint of blue, and the other fins are mostly clear or only slightly dusky.
